title: Anokye v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration)
frame:
Forum: Federal Court.
Parties as styled: applicant = LORETTA ANOKYE; respondent = THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION.
Decision under review (from the opening paragraphs): The applicant had already completed the online portion of the program and paid nearly two-thirds of her total program fees before submitting her study permit application in order to complete the in-person clinical training in Vancouver between January and June, 2026.
How the layers nest here: The judge is the author (layer 1). The applicant and respondent in this proceeding make submissions to the judge (layer 2). The decision under review was made by an earlier decision-maker (layer 3), and that decision may itself report what a claimant, the Minister or a witness said to that decision-maker (layer 4).

paragraphs.text: The applicant is a 34-year-old citizen of Ghana. In April 2025, she applied for a study permit in order to pursue the Internationally Educated Midwives Bridging Program (IEMBP) at the University of British Columbia. The applicant was already working as a Senior Staff Midwife at a hospital in Ghana and planned to take a one-year unpaid leave of absence from her position. She explained in her study permit application that the program would provide her with valuable skills and training that she would be able to apply when she returned to Ghana to continue working as a midwife.

The IEMBP is a hybrid program where students are required to complete 12 weeks of online courses followed by at least 22 weeks of clinical placements in Vancouver. The applicant had already completed the online portion of the program and paid nearly two-thirds of her total program fees before submitting her study permit application in order to complete the in-person clinical training in Vancouver between January and June, 2026.

On May 12, 2025, a visa officer with Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada refused the application because the officer was not satisfied that the applicant would leave Canada at the end of her authorized stay, as required by paragraph 216(10(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Regulations, SOR/2002-227.

The applicant now applies for judicial review of this decision under subsection 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (IRPA). She contends that the decision is unreasonable. As I will explain, I do not agree.

The parties agree, as do I, that the substance of the officer’s decision is to be reviewed on a reasonableness standard. Reasonableness review aims to reinforce a “culture of justification” requiring an administrative decision maker to provide an explanation for the result that is “based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at paras 2 and 85). To set aside the decision on the basis that it is unreasonable, the reviewing court must be satisfied that “there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency” (Vavilov, at para 100).

The key principles that guide judicial review of study permit decisions on a reasonableness standard are well established: see Jafarkhani v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2024 FC 1633 at para 5 and the cases cited therein. These principles include the following: The onus is on an applicant to satisfy the officer that they meet the legal requirements for obtaining a study permit, including that they will leave Canada at the end of their authorized stay. Visa officers must consider the “push” and “pull” factors that could, on the one hand, lead an applicant to overstay their visa and remain in Canada or that would, on the other hand, encourage them to return to their home country when required to. In assessing the reasonableness of the decision, the administrative context in which it was made must be taken into account. This includes the high volume of applications to be processed, the nature of the interests involved, and the fact that often an applicant can simply reapply. In and of itself, there is nothing wrong with decision makers using templates to prepare their reasons, as long as the reasons given, when read in their legal and factual context, provide a reasonable explanation for the decision (Ekpenyong v Canada (Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship), 2019 FC 1245 at paras 22-23). Reasons do not need to be lengthy or detailed. Nevertheless, they must set out the key elements of the officer’s line of analysis and be responsive to the central aspects of the application. The decision maker must “justify to the affected party, in a manner that is transparent and intelligible, the basis on which it arrived at a particular conclusion” (Vavilov, at para 96). Even if the outcome may be justifiable, “it is not ordinarily appropriate for the reviewing court to fashion its own reasons in order to buttress the administrative decision” or to “disregard the flawed basis for a decision and substitute its own justification for the outcome” (Vavilov, at para 96).

As noted, the officer refused the study permit application because the officer was not satisfied that the applicant would leave Canada at the end of her authorized stay. The officer based this conclusion on two findings.

First, the officer found that the purpose of the applicant’s visit was not consistent with a temporary stay given the details she had provided in her application. More particularly, the applicant had not established the rationale for leaving her current stable employment as a senior midwife in order to pursue this new credential at high financial cost. As well, the applicant had not established that this credential would provide her with an employment benefit in Ghana.

Second, the officer found that applicant had not established that her assets and financial situation were sufficient to support her proposed studies in Canada. The applicant’s husband had undertaken to cover the costs of the applicant’s studies. To demonstrate that they had the means to fund her studies in Canada, the applicant provided financial information that included the following: (1) a statement for a joint bank account with Ecobank from December 2024 to March 2025 showing transactions over that period and a final balance of $34,185.12 (USD); (2) Eurobond holdings in the amount of $57,981 (USD); and (3) Treasury Bill investments equivalent to $102,769 (CAD). The applicant also provided proof that she had pre-paid $5,635 towards the $9,500 total program fee. The officer found, however, that there was no evidence of how the applicant’s husband came to accumulate either the Eurobond holdings or the Treasury Bill savings. The officer wrote: “In the absence of satisfactory documentation showing the source of these funds, I am not satisfied that the applicant will have sufficient funds for the intended international study.”
The applicant submits that these findings are unreasonable but I do not agree.

Looking first at the applicant’s reasons for wishing to undertake the IEMBP, it should be noted that, as the letter of acceptance submitted by the applicant made clear, the program is designed to train internationally educated midwives for practice in Canada. Significantly, the IEMBP is a non-credit program and it does not issue academic transcripts or attendance records. Instead, upon successful completion, a completion form is sent to the British Columbia College of Midwives confirming that the student has met all the requirements to be eligible to register with the college. While the applicant said in her study plan that the program would benefit her practice as a midwife in Ghana, she did not directly address the fact that it is meant for midwives who want to practice in Canada. As well, there was little evidence that the program actually taught many of the subjects and skills the applicant said she hoped to learn through the program or how the program would meaningfully add to what the applicant had already learned through her training and work experience in Ghana.

The officer could certainly have said more about why they were not satisfied with the applicant’s reasons for wanting to pursue this particular program but, given the information the applicant had presented in her study permit application, the reasons that were given are sufficient to explain the officer’s finding in a way that is transparent, intelligible and justified.

Second, it was not unreasonable for the officer to be concerned about the sufficiency of the funds that would be available to support the applicant’s studies in Canada given the complete absence of evidence as to the provenance of a significant portion of the funds the applicant relied on in her application. While the applicant’s husband stated in his affidavit that he was “financially sound to bear my wife’s entire financial expenses during her stay in Canada,” there was no evidence as to how this was the case – not even whether he was employed. Moreover, while the applicant herself had been employed as a midwife since July 2019, there was no evidence of the income she earned in that position. Again, while the officer could have said more about this, I am satisfied that what the officer did say, when read in light of the information before the officer, was sufficient to explain their finding.

The applicant also submits that it was unreasonable for the officer to be concerned about the provenance of the Eurobond holdings and Treasury Bill investments because the funds in the joint bank account alone would be sufficient to cover the costs of her studies in Canada. I do not agree. Even if it were true that the joint bank account funds were sufficient (something that is far from obvious given the absence of any evidence of the family’s regular expenses), that is not how the study permit application was presented to the officer. With the applicant herself having seen fit to rely on the additional sources of funds, it was not unreasonable for the officer to scrutinize those funds. Nor was it unreasonable for the officer to find that the evidence that those funds would be available to the applicant was insufficient. While the officer did not comment directly on the sufficiency of the funds in the joint bank account alone, they were never asked to do so. The failure to address the sufficiency of those funds on their own does not undermine the reasonableness of the decision given the financial picture presented by the applicant in support of the study permit application.

The applicant was no doubt disappointed with the officer’s decision but she can always apply again for a study permit. If she does, and if she is able to provide evidence that addresses the concerns raised by this officer, she may well be able to satisfy another officer that a study permit should be issued. The applicant has not, however, established any basis on which to interfere with the decision under review. This application for judicial review must, therefore, be dismissed.

The parties did not propose any serious questions of general importance for certification under paragraph 74(d) of the IRPA. I agree that no question arises. JUDGMENT IN IMM-12386-25 THIS COURT’S JUDGMENT is that The application for judicial review is dismissed. No question of general importance is stated. “John Norris” Judge FEDERAL COURT SOLICITORS OF RECORD DOCKET: IMM-12386-25 STYLE OF CAUSE: LORETTA ANOKYE v THE MINISTER OF CITIZENSHIP AND IMMIGRATION PLACE OF HEARING: HELD BY VIDEOCONFERENCE DATE OF HEARING: September 15, 2026 REASONS AND JUDGMENT: NORRIS J.
